sections.heading: Abstract
paragraphs: This reading covers the Italian edition of Solana's white paper on a high-performance blockchain architecture, version v0.8.14. The body paragraphs were written from the Italian PDF text extract alone and were not compared sentence-by-sentence with the English edition for translation fidelity. Anatoly Yakovenko is the listed author. The opening legal disclaimer says nothing in the paper is an offer to sell tokens and that Solana publishes it only for public feedback.

The Italian abstract bases the architecture on Proof of History for verifying order and the passage of time between events, encoding secure time passage into an append-only ledger. Used with Proof of Work or Proof of Stake, PoH is argued to reduce messaging overhead in a Byzantine fault-tolerant replicated state machine with finalization times under a second. Two further algorithms exploit PoH timekeeping: a Proof of Stake rule that recovers from partitions of any size, and an efficient streaming Proof of Replication. PoRep plus PoH defend against forging time ordering and storage. On a 1 gbps network the paper claims up to 710k transactions per second with today's hardware.

sections.heading: 1 Introduzione
paragraphs: Blockchain is the implementation of a fault-tolerant replicated state machine. Blockchains currently available to the public do not rely on time, or make a weak hypothesis about a participant's ability to keep time. Each node in the network usually relies on its own local clock without other participants knowing that clock. Lack of a trusted time source means that when a message timestamp is used to accept or reject a message, there is no guarantee every other participant will make the exact same choice. The PoH presented here was designed to create a ledger with verifiable passage of time—duration between events and message ordering—so every node can rely on the recorded passage of time without trust.

sections.heading: 2 Indice
paragraphs: The remainder of the article is organized as follows. Overall system design is described in Section 3. An in-depth description of Proof of History is in Section 4. An in-depth description of the proposed Proof of Stake consensus algorithm is in Section 5. An in-depth description of the proposed fast Proof of Replication is in Section 6. System architecture and performance limits are analyzed in Section 7. A high-performance GPU-friendly smart-contracts engine is described in Section 7.5.

sections.heading: 3 Network Design
paragraphs: As in Figure 1, some system node is Leader and produces the Proof of History sequence that gives global read consistency and verifiable time. The Leader sequences user messages for efficient processing, runs them on RAM-resident state, and publishes transactions with a final-state signature to Verifier replication nodes. Verifiers execute the same transactions and publish computed state signatures as confirmations used as consensus votes.

Without a partition there is one Leader. Every Verifier has Leader-equivalent hardware and can be elected Leader via Proof of Stake elections covered in Section 5.6. CAP framing prefers consistency over availability when partitioned, and the paper proposes recovering network control from a partition of any size, with detail deferred to Section 5.12.

sections.heading: 4 Proof of History
paragraphs: Proof of History is an iterated computation meant to let anyone cryptographically check how much time separates two events. It uses a secure function whose output cannot be guessed from the input and that must run to completion before any digest is produced. The loop remains pinned to a single core: each prior output becomes the next input, and the current output plus call count are recorded periodically. Outside machines can recompute and check the chain in parallel by assigning each segment to its own core.

Events are stamped by mixing data, or a digest of data, into the function state. Recording state, index, and appended material places the event before the next hash in the sequence. Multiple generators can scale sideways by folding each other's state into their sequences, a topic returned to in Section 4.4.

sections.heading: 4.1 Description
paragraphs: The construction starts from a cryptographic hash such as sha256 or ripemd whose result cannot be known before the function runs. From a random seed the function is applied repeatedly, feeding each digest into the next call, while recording call counts and outputs. The seed may be any public string; the text mentions a newspaper headline as an example of an acceptable starting value.

Because predicting the next digest without running the prior step is infeasible, the recorded sequence is offered as evidence that real time passed between recorded indices. Verification does not need a single serial replay: given recorded checkpoints, many cores can recompute disjoint intervals at once and confirm that each segment matches the published hashes. The same section stresses that the generator runs serially on one core while verification fans out, which is why a comparatively slow producer can still be audited quickly by well-equipped verifiers.

sections.heading: 4.2 Timestamp for Events
paragraphs: Any event can be mixed into the running state so that the next hash commits to that event's presence at that index. Clients may insert raw bytes or a digest of larger payloads. Table 1 in the text illustrates two photograph digests inserted at distinct counters so later readers see a forced ordering between those events.

Once an event's digest is inside the sequence, every later hash depends on it. Claiming the event happened after a later index would require finding a colliding continuation of the hash chain, which the paper treats as intractable for the chosen function.

Observers who hold the recorded checkpoints can argue both that some real work separated two indices and that a named event sat between them. Soft clients are warned not to assume perfect ordering inside the short window between the last hash they observed and the moment their own event is included.

The section also notes that signed client payloads can bind an event to the last observed hash so a malicious generator cannot quietly rewrite client-submitted digests without breaking signatures. Verification then checks both the signature and that the referenced prior hash actually appears earlier in the published sequence.

sections.heading: 4.3 Verifica
paragraphs: Verification splits the published sequence into contiguous segments whose endpoints are known hashes and counters. Each segment is assigned to a separate core or GPU lane. Modern GPU examples in the text cite on the order of four thousand cores, so a long serial production run can be checked in a small fraction of the production time.

Correctness requires every segment to recompute to the published terminal hash. A single mismatched segment falsifies the whole claim for that interval. The text present this parallel check as the practical reason Proof of History can be produced slowly yet audited quickly across the network.

sections.heading: 4.4 Scaling Orizzontale
paragraphs: Several Proof of History generators may run at once if they periodically mix observed hashes from peer generators into their own sequences. After such a mix, events in one stream gain a cryptographic before-or-after relation to events in another through the shared mixed state. Synchronization is described as transitive: if A mixes with B and B mixes with C, then A and C obtain a provable event order through B. Bold highlighting in the figures marks the mixed hashes that create those bridges.

The cost of this fan-out is availability. The paper's worked arithmetic says ten independent 1 gbps links each at 0.999 availability would compound to roughly 0.999 to the tenth, or about 0.99 overall, when the design requires all paths. Horizontal scaling therefore trades connectivity risk for higher aggregate sequencing capacity across synchronized generators.

sections.heading: 4.5 Consistenza
paragraphs: Clients strengthen consistency by embedding the latest hash they accept as valid into the events they submit. A malicious generator that holds every pending event could otherwise build a hidden alternate sequence that reverses order, especially if it can compute a hidden chain faster than the public one.

By forcing Event1 to cite hash10a, Event2 to cite the hash after Event1, and so on consumers who later see a published stream can reject any rearrangement that breaks those back-references. Partial reordering attacks then shrink to the short hash window between observation and inclusion.

Clients may further sign the concatenation of event data and the last observed hash. Verification then checks the signature under the client's key and looks up the cited prior hash inside the official sequence, blocking silent rewrite of client digests by the generator. Figure 6 sketches inputs that carry those back references, and the surrounding prose treats this client-assisted binding as the main consistency tool against a dishonest PoH producer.

sections.heading: 4.6 Generalità
paragraphs: Recording checkpoints and mixing peer hashes adds modest computational and bandwidth cost relative to bare hashing. The text place the practical overhead discussion next to GPU verification figures on the order of 0.25–0.75 milliseconds when thousands of cores recompute segments, presenting that cost as acceptable beside the messaging savings claimed for consensus.

sections.heading: 4.7 Attacchi
paragraphs: The attack subsection enumerates ways an adversary might try to reverse event order, outrun honest generators, or rebuild history from a distant past. Each named attack is answered with a short mitigation that leans on the hash-chain properties, client back-references, or the stake and replication layers introduced later.

sections.heading: 4.7.1 Reversal
paragraphs: A reversal attack tries to publish events in an order different from the one clients experienced. Because honest clients embed recent hashes into signed submissions, a reordered stream fails lookup checks when cited predecessors are missing. The residual risk is limited to the brief interval of hashes produced while a client's event was in flight.

sections.heading: 4.7.2 Velocità
paragraphs: If an attacker can evaluate the hash function faster than the elected generator, a hidden faster chain becomes possible. The paper answers that verification is parallel and that consensus stake, not raw hash speed alone, elects who may publish the authoritative stream, so a faster ASIC does not automatically win leadership without stake and votes.

sections.heading: 4.7.3 Attacchi a lungo raggio
paragraphs: A long-range rewrite would start from an old checkpoint and attempt to grow an alternate history faster than the honest chain. Because each step is sequential and unpredictable, catching up requires sustained hashing faster than the live generator over the entire gap. The text treats that requirement as economically and practically hard when the live stream keeps advancing and when stake-weighted votes continually ratify recent hashes, leaving long-range forks recognizable as slower or unsupported histories.

sections.heading: 5 Proof of Stake Consensus
paragraphs: Proof of Stake here elects and disciplines the Proof of History generator using bonded capital. Validators lock stake, vote on state hashes carried in the PoH stream, and risk slashing when they support contradictory or invalid histories. The chapter also covers elections, secondary generators, availability under partition, recovery, and finality.

sections.heading: 5.1 Descrizione
paragraphs: Validators bond tokens to gain voting weight proportional to stake. They watch the Leader's PoH stream, recompute state, and publish votes that confirm particular state hashes at particular PoH indices. Supermajority confirmation is what advances the canonical branch; conflicting votes against the same stake invite slashing penalties described later.

sections.heading: 5.2 Terminologia
paragraphs: Bonding locks stake behind a validator identity for a period. Voting is a signed statement that a named state hash is correct at a PoH counter. Unbonding starts a delay before stake can exit so that slashable misbehavior discovered after the fact can still be punished. Branches are competing PoH histories; the heaviest confirmed branch is preferred. Secondary and lower generators are standby identities that may take over if the active PoH identity fails or forks. Election triggers, timeouts, and slashing conditions are defined so validators know when to switch allegiance and when bonds are forfeit.

sections.heading: 5.3 Bonding
paragraphs: To join consensus a validator submits a bonding transaction that locks stake and announces a voting identity. Bonds remain active until an unbonding flow completes. Active bonds grant vote weight and also expose that stake to slashing if the validator confirms mutually inconsistent or demonstrably false state hashes.

sections.heading: 5.4 Voto
paragraphs: Votes are ordinary transactions inside the PoH stream. A validator signs the state hash that results after replaying all transactions up to a chosen index and publishes that signature. Looking at consecutive votes in the ledger shows how much PoH time separates confirmations, which later sections use when arguing about finality and timeouts.

sections.heading: 5.5 Unbonding
paragraphs: Unbonding begins when a validator signals exit. Stake stays locked through a delay measured in PoH time so that evidence of prior double-voting or confirmation of invalid hashes can still slash the bond. Only after the delay and any pending challenges clear does the capital become transferable again.

sections.heading: 5.6 Elezioni
paragraphs: A new PoH generator is elected when failure of the current one is detected. The validator with the greatest voting power, or the next according to the stated tie rules, becomes the new generator. Changing a prior vote requires casting a replacement on a higher PoH sequence and including the votes being superseded. Once a generator is established, validators may also designate an alternate that stands ready under the secondary-election rules. Scheduled or exception-driven handoffs keep a successor identity ready without waiting for a full cold start after every fault.

sections.heading: 5.7 Election Triggers
paragraphs: Elections fire when the active generator's identity publishes conflicting histories, when runtime exceptions show the producer is faulty, or when network timeouts indicate the stream has stalled. Each trigger is expanded in the following subsections so operators can automate failover.

sections.heading: 5.7.1 Fork di un Generatore Proof of History
paragraphs: PoH generators sign their sequences under a durable identity. A fork appears when two different historical records are published under that same identity, which the paper says can happen only if the signing key is compromised. Validators who see divergent signed streams treat that as an immediate election trigger.

sections.heading: 5.7.2 Eccezioni di Runtime
paragraphs: Hardware faults, bugs, or intentional misbehavior inside the generator can emit invalid hashes or crash the producer. Validators gossip the correct signatures they compute locally; persistent mismatch or crash evidence elevates the elected secondary and starts a new primary election under the stake rules.

sections.heading: 5.7.3 Network Timeouts
paragraphs: If votes or PoH packets stop arriving within the configured timeout measured against local observation of the stream, validators conclude the leader is unreachable. They then open an election for a replacement generator according to stake ranking so the network can resume producing a signed Proof of History sequence without waiting indefinitely on a silent primary.

sections.heading: 5.8 Slashing
paragraphs: Slashing burns or locks bonded stake when a validator confirms contradictory branches or endorses an invalid hash that the PoH generator planted as a trap. Evidence is itself a transaction that points at the conflicting signed votes. The design expects random invalid hashes from the honest generator so idle validators who rubber-stamp without checking lose stake, which underpins the tragedy-of-the-commons defense developed later in the chapter.

sections.heading: 5.9 Elezioni secondarie
paragraphs: Secondary and lower-ranked generators can be nominated and confirmed in advance so failover is orderly. When the primary fails, stake weight already pointing at the secondary shortens the window without a live PoH stream. Secondaries still must produce valid sequences once elevated; failing that the next ranked candidate is elected under the same fork, exception, and timeout triggers that apply to the primary.

sections.heading: 5.10 Disponibilità
paragraphs: Availability discusses how the network keeps a usable ledger when many validators disappear. Votes that confirm state hashes continue as PoH transactions, and observers can measure gaps between votes directly from counters in the stream. Large partitions may leave only a minority online; the paper argues that time kept inside PoH still lets the surviving set reason about how long the minority has been confirming a branch before wider reunification. Configuration knobs such as minimum bond sizes and replication identity rules further shape how much capital must remain online for the partition to keep finalizing under the stated thresholds.

sections.heading: 5.11 Recupero
paragraphs: Recovery explains how control returns after partitions of arbitrary size. Validators compare PoH-backed histories, slash contradictory bonds where evidence exists, and converge on the branch that gathers supermajority stake once communication resumes. Full restoration with zero validators initially available is described as taking a sequence of bonding and confirmation steps until stake weight again crosses the finality threshold on one history.

sections.heading: 5.12 Finalità
paragraphs: Finality arrives when a supermajority of bonded stake has confirmed a state hash at a PoH index and conflicting votes would be slashable. Because PoH orders the votes themselves, observers can see confirmation accumulate in time rather than waiting on unbounded message rounds alone.

sections.heading: 5.13 Attacchi
paragraphs: The consensus attack catalog covers free-riding validators, collusion with the PoH producer, censorship of users or voters, long-range history rewrites, and ASIC-assisted leadership grabs. Each subsection pairs the threat with an economic or cryptographic countermeasure already embedded in bonding, voting, or PoH.

sections.heading: 5.13.1 Tragedia dei beni comuni
paragraphs: Validators might skip verifying state and simply echo the leader's hashes to save work. The countermeasure is random invalid hashes inserted by the PoH generator; anyone who votes for them is slashable, and the network should immediately promote the elected secondary generator. That random trap creates a private incentive to verify even when public goods alone would under-provide checking effort across the bonded set.

sections.heading: 5.13.2 Collusione con il lgeneratore PoH
paragraphs: A validator who colludes with the generator might learn when invalid trap hashes will appear. The paper equates that advantage with the generator itself holding large verifier stake: the producer must still compute honest state hashes for the rest of the stream, and stake-weighted votes remain visible and slashable if they endorse contradictions.

sections.heading: 5.13.3 Censura
paragraphs: A censoring leader could omit disfavored transactions or votes from the PoH stream. Clients and validators detect censorship when messages that gossip successfully never appear after enough PoH time, which becomes grounds to favor a secondary generator who includes them. Because votes travel as transactions, censoring votes is visible as missing confirmations relative to stake that is known to be online, accelerating election triggers against the censoring identity.

sections.heading: 5.13.4 Attacchi a lungo raggio
paragraphs: Long-range attackers try to rebuild from old stake distributions. PoH forces them to hash sequentially from the fork point; without outrunning the live generator they cannot present a denser time record. Slashable bonds and delayed unbonding further shrink the set of stake that could be reused quietly in a rewritten past while honest voters keep confirming the live tip.

sections.heading: 5.13.5 Attacchi ASIC
paragraphs: ASIC risk appears when specialized hardware could dominate hash production during partitions or elections. The protocol answers by separating verification, which parallelizes on commodity GPUs, from leadership, which requires stake-weighted votes rather than raw hash power alone. Even a fast ASIC identity still needs bonded capital and confirmations; producing a longer hidden chain without votes does not by itself move finality under the stated rules.

sections.heading: 6 Prova di Replicazione in Streaming
paragraphs: Streaming Proof of Replication proves that replicas store ledger data without forcing slow interactive challenges. Combined with PoH it aims to defend both the time ordering of the ledger and the claim that historical bytes remain stored. The chapter covers the CBC-CBC-style construction, verification, key rotation, hash selection, validation, and attacks.

sections.heading: 6.1 Descrizione
paragraphs: Replicas encrypt or encode ledger slices under keys tied to their identity and must stream proofs that specific chunks remain retrievable. PoH timestamps when proofs were generated so verifiers can demand fresh evidence rather than accepting precomputed answers prepared offline at leisure.

sections.heading: 6.2 Algoritmo
paragraphs: The algorithm seals data in layers so that opening a proof requires touching storage in a prescribed order. Keys derive from replica identity and PoH-linked material, binding proofs to both who claims storage and when the proof was built. Streaming means proofs can be emitted continuously as the ledger grows instead of waiting for rare audit epochs. Validators sample proofs as transactions or gossip payloads and reject replicas that cannot answer within the expected PoH window. Specific sealing steps follow the Filecoin-influenced Proof of Replication lineage cited in the references, adapted so challenges align with counters already present in the Solana PoH stream.

sections.heading: 6.3 Verifica
paragraphs: Verifiers recompute the cheap open steps of a submitted proof and check them against the sealed commitment and the PoH time when the challenge was issued. Failed proofs slash or disqualify the replica under the consensus configuration. Because challenges reference recent PoH hashes, proofs generated long in advance cannot satisfy fresh challenges without holding the data at challenge time, which is the property that makes streaming audits meaningful.

sections.heading: 6.4 Rotazione delle chiavi
paragraphs: Replica keys rotate on a PoH-driven schedule so that compromising an old key does not let an attacker keep answering new challenges forever. Rotation forces resealing or re-encoding under the new key within a bounded number of counters, limiting how long stolen credentials remain useful for forging storage proofs against live challenges.

sections.heading: 6.5 Selezione degli Hash
paragraphs: Challenges pick hash locations using entropy from the PoH stream so neither the replica nor a colluding leader can predict distant future sample points. Unpredictable selection undercuts grinding for easy blocks. Selection coverage is argued to make partial storage statistically visible once enough challenges accumulate against a replica that has erased cold chunks.

sections.heading: 6.6 Convalida della prova
paragraphs: Validation accepts a proof only if cryptographic checks pass and the proof cites a sufficiently recent PoH hash. Stale proofs are ignored even if otherwise well-formed. Consensus validators record validation outcomes so replication targets that miss too many challenges lose approval and where configured, stake tied to those identities.

sections.heading: 6.7 Attacchi
paragraphs: Replication attacks include spam floods of fake proofs, erasing only part of stored data, colluding with the PoH leader to learn challenges early, denial-of-service against honest replicas, and tragedy-of-the-commons laziness among validators who skip checking proofs. Each named case receives a dedicated countermeasure in the subsections that follow.

sections.heading: 6.7.1 Spam
paragraphs: Spam submits many proofs to exhaust verifier bandwidth. Mitigation ties proof submission to bonded identities and rate limits derived from stake or minimum bond configuration so unbound floods are cheap to ignore. Invalid proofs that still consume CPU are discouraged by requiring cheap preliminary checks before heavier validation work begins.

sections.heading: 6.7.2 Cancellazione Parziale
paragraphs: An adversary may delete rarely sampled chunks while keeping hot pieces. Random PoH-driven sampling makes long-term partial erasure detectable with high probability as challenges continue. Once a missing chunk is proven, the replica can be slashed or voted out of the approved replication set so it no longer earns credit for storage it does not hold.

sections.heading: 6.7.3 Collusione con il generatore di Proof of History
paragraphs: Collusion might leak upcoming challenge hashes to a replica so it materializes only those blocks. Frequent key rotation and binding challenges to hashes the colluding leader cannot uniquely predict far ahead shrink that window. Validators can also demand occasional false proofs for short periods and slash Proof of Stake confirmers who accept them, as the text describes near the close of the attack discussion.

sections.heading: 6.7.4 Rifiuto del Servizio
paragraphs: Flooding replicas or verifiers with traffic can stall honest proofs. Diversified replication targets and Reed-Solomon striping mentioned in the network-limits chapter give alternate paths for ledger data when some nodes are saturated. Stake-weighted approval of replication identities lets the network drop targets that stay unreachable beyond PoH timeouts.

sections.heading: 6.7.5 Tragedia dei Beni Comuni
paragraphs: Validators might accept replication proofs without checking. The paper's counter is economic: false proofs can be revealed by showing the function that generated fake data, and any Proof of Stake validator who confirmed a false proof is slashed. Random false-proof drills further keep validators honest about performing validation work rather than free-riding on others' diligence.

sections.heading: 7 Architettura di Sistema
paragraphs: Section 7 inventories the deployed roles—Leader, state tables, Verifiers, and Validators—then analyzes network, compute, and memory ceilings that motivate the headline throughput numbers. The chapter closes with the extended Berkeley Packet Filter smart-contract engine aimed at GPU-friendly batch execution of intrinsics.

sections.heading: 7.1 Componenti
paragraphs: Components are the Leader PoH generator, the in-memory state tables indexed by user addresses, Verifier nodes that replicate state, and Validator nodes that consume verifier bandwidth for consensus voting. Each role can colocate or run on separate machines depending on configuration.

sections.heading: 7.1.1 Leader, Generatore Proof of History
paragraphs: The Leader is the elected Proof of History generator. It consumes arbitrary user transactions, emits a PoH sequence that fixes a unique global order, and after each batch publishes a signature of the resulting state under the Leader identity so Verifiers can compare results.

sections.heading: 7.1.2 Stato
paragraphs: State is a simple hash table keyed by user address. Each cell stores the full user address material needed for the computation. The transaction table example packs a RIPEMD digest of the account public key with account fields into thirty-two bytes altogether. The Proof of Stake bond table stores a RIPEMD digest of the account holder's public key together with bond amount and most recent vote, occupying 64 bytes in the layout the text diagrams.

sections.heading: 7.1.3 Verificatore, Replicazione di stato
paragraphs: Verifier nodes replicate blockchain state for high availability. The consensus algorithm selects replication targets, and consensus validators vote for Proof of Replication nodes they approve using off-chain criteria. Networks may set a minimum Proof of Stake bond size and require a unique replicator identity per bond.

sections.heading: 7.1.4 Validatori
paragraphs: Validators consume bandwidth from Verifiers. They are virtual nodes that may run on the same machines as Verifiers or the Leader, or on separate machines dedicated to the consensus algorithm configured for that network, depending on how operators choose to colocate roles.

sections.heading: 7.2 Limiti di Rete
paragraphs: The Leader must ingest user packets, order them for favorable memory access to cut faults (per the file) and improve prefetching, and publish them in a Proof of History sequence to downstream Verifiers. Incoming packet layouts enumerate fields for last (per the file) valid hash, counter, fees, source, and signatures. Without payload the signed packet size is given as 20 + 8 (per the file) + 16 + 8 + 32 + 32 + 32 = 148 bytes. The minimum supported payload with one destination account is (per the file) 176 bytes, which becomes the denominator in the throughput arithmetic.

The Proof of History output packet carries the current hash, counter, hash of newly added messages, and the signed state after processing, sent once every N messages. Its minimum size is listed as 132 bytes. On a 1 gbps link the maximum transaction count is computed as 1 gigabit per second divided by 176 bytes, equaling 710k tps maximum. About 1–4% loss is expected from Ethernet framing. Spare capacity beyond the target payload can raise availability by Reed-Solomon encoding outputs and striping them across available downstream Verifiers.

sections.heading: 7.3 Limiti Computazionali
paragraphs: Each transaction needs a signature digest check that touches little memory beyond the message and parallelizes freely, so throughput is bounded by available cores. GPU-based ECDSA verification servers are cited with experimental results around 900k operations per second, which the analysis treats as evidence that signature checking need not be the binding constraint beside the network arithmetic.

sections.heading: 7.4 Limiti di Memoria
paragraphs: A naive half-full hash table with 32-byte entries could theoretically hold 10 billion accounts in 640 GB. Steady random access to that table is measured at 1.1 times 10 to the seventh reads or writes per second. At two reads and two writes per transaction, memory can sustain about 2.75 million transactions per second on the measured Amazon Web Services 1 TB x1.16xlarge-class instance named in the text.

sections.heading: 7.5 Smart Contracts ad alte Performance
paragraphs: Smart contracts generalize transactions into programs every node runs to mutate state. The design uses extended Berkeley Packet Filter bytecode for speed and analyzability, with JIT bytecode as the contract language, and claims zero-cost foreign-function calls into platform intrinsics. Calling an intrinsic suspends the user program and schedules the intrinsic on a high-performance server; intrinsics are batched for parallel GPU execution.

Two user programs may call the same intrinsic and both stay paused until the batch finishes. ECDSA verification is the worked intrinsic, with GPU batching claimed to multiply throughput by thousands. Figure 11 concerns BPF program execution. The trampoline needs no native OS thread context switch because BPF already defines its memory context.

An eBPF LLVM backend has existed since 2015, so any LLVM frontend language can author contracts; Linux has carried the bytecode since 2015, with earlier forms dating to 1992. A single pass can check eBPF correctness, settle runtime and memory needs, and lower it to x86 instructions for execution on ordinary validators.
